title: Ronin bridge validator key compromise
body: The Ronin bridge required five of nine validator signatures to authorise a withdrawal. Four validator keys were held by Sky Mavis infrastructure and a fifth was delegated to the Axie DAO during a period of high load; the allowlist entry was never revoked after the load subsided. An attacker who obtained access to the Sky Mavis nodes therefore controlled five keys and signed two withdrawals draining 173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC. The compromise went unnoticed for six days because no independent monitor compared bridge liabilities against locked collateral.

title: Wormhole signature verification bypass on Solana
body: The Solana side of the Wormhole bridge verified guardian signatures through a system instruction, but the verification routine used a deprecated function that did not confirm the account passed in was the genuine sysvar instructions account. The attacker supplied a spoofed account, produced a message that passed verification with no valid guardian signatures, and minted 120,000 wrapped ETH against no deposit. A fix had been committed to the public repository but not yet deployed, and the commit itself disclosed the flaw.

title: Euler donateToReserves broke the liquidation health invariant
body: The donateToReserves function let an account transfer its own eTokens to the protocol reserve without any check that the account remained solvent afterwards. The attacker used a flash loan to build a leveraged position, donated enough to push itself deep underwater in one call, then self liquidated. Because the soft liquidation discount scales with how unhealthy a position is, the discount on a position made arbitrarily unhealthy in a single transaction was large enough to extract far more collateral than the debt cleared.

title: Beanstalk governance takeover with flash loaned voting power
body: Beanstalk counted governance weight from the current stalk balance rather than from a snapshot taken before the proposal existed. The attacker submitted a proposal, waited for the emergency commit window to mature, then flash borrowed roughly one billion dollars of liquidity from Aave and Uniswap, deposited it for stalk, passed their own proposal with a supermajority, and executed a payload that transferred the protocol treasury to themselves, all inside one transaction and one block.

title: Nomad bridge accepted every message after a bad initialisation
body: A routine upgrade initialised the trusted root of the Replica contract to the zero value. The proving routine treated a message whose stored root equalled the zero value as proven, so any message at all passed validation. Once the first attacker demonstrated the pattern, hundreds of copycats replayed the same calldata with their own address substituted, and the bridge was emptied in a chaotic open access drain over several hours. The root cause was an upgrade parameter, not a logic flaw in the proving code itself.

title: Mango Markets oracle price manipulation on a thin market
body: The attacker funded two accounts, took the long and short sides of an outsized MNGO perpetual position against themselves, then bought MNGO spot across every venue the oracle referenced. The token was thin enough that a few million dollars moved the reported price by more than an order of magnitude, marking the long position to a paper profit that the protocol treated as collateral. The attacker borrowed every other asset in the treasury against that mark and left the platform with bad debt.

title: Cream Finance yUSD price oracle manipulated through a direct donation
body: Cream priced yUSD collateral from the yVault pricePerShare, which is computed as the vault balance divided by total supply. The attacker flash borrowed, donated a large amount of the underlying straight into the vault to double pricePerShare, and borrowed against the now doubled collateral valuation. Any oracle derived from a mutable contract balance rather than from an accounting variable inherits this weakness, and the same shape recurred in several later incidents.

title: bZx flash loan attack combining a thin oracle and missing slippage limits
body: The attacker flash borrowed ETH, used part of it to open a leveraged short on bZx that the protocol executed on Uniswap with no slippage bound, and used the rest to move the sUSD price on Kyber, which bZx consulted as its oracle. The manipulated price let the position be opened against collateral it did not have. This was the first widely analysed flash loan attack and established the pattern of borrowing capital to move a price and a position in the same atomic transaction.

title: Compound Proposal 62 distributed COMP to every user through a wrong comparison
body: A governance upgrade meant to fix reward accrual introduced a comparison against the wrong accrual variable in the Comptroller. Instead of paying rewards proportionally, the contract paid the whole accrued amount to any account that called claimComp. There was no admin path to pause the distribution, and a fix had to pass the full seven day governance cycle while roughly eighty million dollars of COMP was claimed. The proposal had been reviewed but the diff was not covered by a test that exercised the claim path.

title: Rari Fuse read only reentrancy through a Curve pool exit
body: Fuse pools priced Curve LP collateral with get_virtual_price. During remove_liquidity the Curve pool sends the native asset to the caller before it updates its own supply, so a callback observes a virtual price computed from a reduced balance against an unreduced supply. The attacker borrowed against that inflated valuation from inside the callback across many Fuse pools. The exploit needed no flash loan of the collateral itself and depended entirely on the ordering inside a dependency.

title: Poly Network keeper role overwritten through a crafted cross chain payload
body: The EthCrossChainManager contract could call any method on the EthCrossChainData contract it owned, and the target method was selected by a function signature carried in the cross chain payload. The attacker brute forced a method name whose four byte selector matched putCurEpochConPubKeyBytes, the function that sets the keeper public keys, and used it to install their own key. From that point every withdrawal they signed was accepted as a legitimate relayed message.

title: Malfunctioning reentrancy lock in three Vyper compiler releases
body: Vyper releases 0.2.15 through 0.3.0 emitted a reentrancy lock that used a different storage slot for each decorated function instead of one shared slot, so the guard did not actually exclude cross function reentrancy. Several Curve stable pools compiled with those versions were drained through the native token callback in remove_liquidity. The vulnerability lived in the compiler rather than in any audited source file, which is why source level review across all the affected protocols did not surface it.
